newsitem.title: GERMANY: POLL - Bundesbank seen keeping steady hand on rates.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Bundesbank seen keeping steady hand on rates.

text.p: The Bundesbank will leave its interest rates unchanged for the rest of this year, a Reuters poll showed on Wednesday, and almost half of those polled also predicted no policy change throughout 1998.

Of a group of 25 forecasters who made predictions through to the final quarter of 1998, nine said the discount rate would remain at its current historic low of 2.50 percent until the Bundesbank hands over monetary policy control to the European Central Bank at the start of 1999.
A further nine saw a rise of 25 or 50 basis points in the rate in the second quarter of 1998, while six predicted a slightly earlier or slightly later move.

Only one forecaster, the Institut fuer Wirtschaft, said the discount rate -- the floor for German money market rates -- would be increased this year, predicting a rise of 20 basis points, or 0.2 of a percentage point, in the final quarter.
On a mean average, the discount rate was seen landing at 2.91 percent at the end of the forecast period at end-1998. The median forecast was 3.0 percent.
The Lombard rate, which is now two percentage points higher than the discount at 4.50 percent, was seen tracking the discount higher.

The relatively steady interest rate forecasts reflected predictions of a stable monetary environment. Inflation was seen edging gradually higher over the next 18 months, but still to no more than two percent.

And M3 money supply -- the Bundesbank's main monetary policy indicator which it believes signals future inflation levels -- was expected to move gradually closer to the Bundesbank's orientation target of five percent growth.
The mean rate of annualised M3 growth, estimated at 6.8 percent in the second quarter of 1997, was seen slowing to 6.0 percent by the end of the forecast period.
In capital markets, 10-year bund yields were seen heading gradually higher over the period, rising overall by around three quarters of a percentage point to about 6.65 percent.
Three-month Frankfurt Interbank Offered Rates (FIBOR) similarly were expected to rise by about 3/4 percentage point, peaking at a mean 3.93 percent in the final quarter of 1998.
